title: Sacraments as instruments (ST III.62)
hook: God uses sacraments like a craftsman uses tools

segments.voice: Yesterday, why God became man: not because he had to, but because it was the fitting way for goodness to share itself. Your line was most fitting. Where did you show up in person? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

A violin lying in its case makes no music. Not a note. Leave it there as long as you like and it's still silent wood and string. Put it in a player's hands and suddenly the room is full. So who made the music? The player, obviously. And yet it's not the player's voice you're hearing. It's the violin's. The sound has the grain of that wood in it. Thomas Aquinas asks a question like this about the sacraments: water, oil, bread, words. Who is really doing the work? His answer turns on a craftsman and a tool.
screen: `A VIOLIN IN ITS CASE IS SILENT.` → `IN A PLAYER'S HANDS, MUSIC.` → `WHO DOES THE WORK?`

segments.voice: Thomas starts by sorting causes into two kinds. A principal cause works by its own power, the way fire heats. An instrumental cause works because something greater is moving it. His picture is a carpenter and an axe. The bed that gets made looks like the plan in the carpenter's head, not like the axe. The axe doesn't know anything about beds. But the carpenter really does work through it. So, Thomas says, God is the principal cause of grace, and the sacraments are his instruments. The water of baptism doesn't hold grace like a jar holds coins. God gives grace through it, the way the carpenter cuts through the axe. Then a detail that makes this more than a metaphor. An instrument, Thomas says, has its own action too. The axe cuts because it's sharp. That's exactly how it serves the carpenter. In the same way, water washes. Bread feeds. Oil soothes. The sign isn't arbitrary: the sacrament's own action is the shape God's work takes. That's why Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, can speak of being saved "by the laver of regeneration, and renovation of the Holy Ghost." A laver is a washing basin. The washing is the instrument; the new life is God's. And one more step. Thomas calls Christ's own humanity an instrument joined to God, like a hand. The sacraments are instruments set apart, like a tool that hand picks up. So grace flows from God, through Christ, through the sacrament, to a person. Christians understand sacraments in different ways; some churches see baptism and the Lord's Supper mainly as signs and acts of obedience. Thomas's picture is that God really works through the tool.
screen: `A PRINCIPAL CAUSE AND AN INSTRUMENT.` · `THE CARPENTER AND THE AXE.` · `THE AXE CUTS BECAUSE IT'S SHARP.` · `A HAND, AND A TOOL IN THE HAND.` · then, large: `THE LAVER OF REGENERATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: handle something with care. Let your shoulders drop. Pick up one ordinary tool within reach: a pen, a cup, a spoon, a key. Hold it slowly. Feel its weight, its edges, what it's made for. Use it once, deliberately: write a word, take a sip, turn the key. Notice how it does what it does: the pen by its ink, the cup by its shape. If you pray, you can ask to be a good tool in God's hands today. Then set it down gently, as if it mattered. The bell holds the time.
Sacraments as instruments. For Thomas, God is the principal cause of grace, and the sacraments are his tools, working by their own action, washing, feeding, anointing. Today's word.
Your line: god's tools. Today, treat one ordinary object, a sink, a loaf, a kitchen knife, with the care a craftsman gives a good tool. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics receive the sacraments as signs through which Christ gives grace, and the Church teaches that they work by the action of Christ himself, not by the holiness of the minister.

fork.setup: does the water of baptism give grace by its own power? what would Thomas say?
options: yes, the water itself is the source.
God gives grace through it, as a carpenter through an axe.
no, the water does nothing at all.
fork.reveal: God is the principal cause; the sacrament is his instrument, and its own action, washing, is how it serves.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a tool, something used to get work done.

trapdoor: what you thought: sacraments are either magic or just symbols.
what it means: for Thomas, God is the principal cause of grace, and sacraments are his instruments.
what a scholar hears: Christ's humanity as a joined instrument, the sacraments as separate instruments, and each with its own proper action.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: principal vs instrumental cause, fire heating, the carpenter and axe, and the bed resembling the craftsman's idea (III.62.1); an instrument has a proper action through which it serves the principal agent, the axe cutting by its sharpness, the water washing the body (62.1 ad 2); Christ's humanity as a conjoined instrument like a hand, the sacraments as separated instruments like a stick (62.5).
'Oil soothes' is a gloss on anointing, not Thomas's example; confirm or change.
Description of other churches ('some churches see baptism and the Lord's Supper mainly as signs and acts of obedience') is brief and unranked; confirm it is fair.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Titus 3:5 (fragment); 'laver' glossed as a washing basin.
